column5: So what does he actually do to you? It starts fast, anywhere from a few hours to a few days after a bad drink.

Most people who catch him barely notice, but they still spread him for days. For the unlucky ones, it begins with sudden, endless, watery diarrhea, so pale that doctors call it rice water. Then the vomiting starts.

The body dries out from the inside. Painful cramps grit the legs. The eyes sink into the skull. The skin on the fingers wrinkles as if you'd been in the bath too long. The blood thickens and the pulse grows weak.
It's nothing personal. I simply need the water more than you do.
And for those who pulled through, usually a full recovery within days, as long as they got enough fluids. But the immunity fades after a few years, so you could catch them again.

For cities, the consequences were enormous. Fear of cholera gave us modern sewers, filtered drinking water, public health boards, and the first international health conferences. Every time you drink clean tap water, you're living in a world he forced us to build.
